lines: – What do you do on Sundays?
items.why: After I the base verb is used: play.

lines: – I ___ up at five every day.
items.why: With I the base form get is used.

lines: – Can you help me with this?
items.why: Negative with I: don't + base verb.
After she the verb takes -s: starts.
With I the form of be is am.
With he the form of be is is.
Parents is plural, so Are comes first.
Age uses be: He is ten.

lines: – What do you have in your bag?
– I have ___ apple and a book.
items.why: Apple starts with a vowel sound, so an.

lines: – Look! ___ sun is very bright today.
items.why: There is only one sun, so we use the.
Jobs take a/an; doctor starts with a consonant sound.

lines: – Is there a bank near here?
– Yes, it is next to ___ hotel.
items.why: Both speakers know which hotel, so the.
She takes the -s form: eats.
With they the base form live is used.
Negative with I: don't + base verb.
He takes -s: works.

lines: – How many children do you have?
items.why: Regular nouns add -s: boys.
Child has an irregular plural: children.

lines: – Do you need anything from the shop?
items.why: Nouns ending in -o like tomato add -es.

lines: – No, I have two ___, and both are black.
items.why: Mouse has an irregular plural: mice.

lines: – It is ___ bag. I am Anna.
items.why: Before a noun we use my, not me.
For a man, the possessive is his.

lines: – Where do you and Ben live?
items.why: Our is the possessive for we.

lines: – Do you like Ana and Luis?
items.why: Their is the possessive for they.
A table is singular, so There is.

lines: – No, we need to buy some.
items.why: Milk is uncountable, so Is there.
Clouds is plural, so there are.
Negative with plural benches: there aren't.
Can does not change with she.
The short negative of can is can't.

lines: – I can't ___; I have a broken arm.
items.why: After can we use the base verb.

lines: – ___ you help me with my homework?
items.why: For a question about ability we put Can first.
The answer is a time, so we ask When.
The answer is a place, so we ask Where.
The answer is a person, so we ask Who.

lines: – ___ do you go to bed so late?
items.why: The answer is a reason (Because), so we ask Why.
An action now uses is + verb-ing.
They needs are + verb-ing.
I needs am + verb-ing for something happening now.
Negative: isn't + verb-ing.
A phone lies on top of a table, so on.
The cat is inside the box, so in.
Clock times use at.
Days use on.
With I we use have got.
With she we use has got.
Question with they: Have they got.
Negative with it: hasn't got.
Regular verbs add -ed in the past: liked.
Past of stay: stayed.
After didn't we use the base verb.
Regular past of clean: cleaned.

lines: – We ___ for ten minutes and then took a taxi.
items.why: Regular past of walk: walked.
Past question: Did + subject + base verb.

lines: – What did you do on Saturday?
items.why: Irregular past of go: went.

lines: – Yes, I ___ him at the bus stop.
items.why: Irregular past of see: saw.

lines: – I ___ my keys and had to go back.
items.why: Irregular past of lose: lost.

lines: – Yes, she ___ it for fifty dollars.
items.why: Irregular past of buy: bought.
Irregular past of eat: ate.

lines: – Did they come to the party?
items.why: Past negative: didn't + base verb.

lines: – What are your plans for tomorrow?
items.why: A plan: am going to + base verb.
A prediction from evidence: is going to.

lines: – Are they moving to a new house?
– Yes, they ___ buy one next month.
items.why: With they: are going to.
Negative: isn't going to + base verb.
Question with you: Are you going to.

lines: – What is she going to do after school?
items.why: She is going to play: is going.
A decision at the moment of speaking: will.

lines: – I think it ___ be sunny tomorrow.
items.why: A prediction (I think) with will + base verb.

lines: – OK, I ___ buy some on my way home.
items.why: An offer made now takes will + base verb.

lines: – Will you be at the party?
items.why: Short negative answer: I won't.
A quick decision to help: will close.

lines: – Will you be at home tonight?
items.why: Will + base verb answers a will question.
With she: has + past participle.
Present perfect: have + past participle (eaten).

lines: – How long have you lived here?
items.why: Since + a point in time takes the present perfect.
With I: haven't + past participle.
Present perfect with they: have + arrived.

lines: – Yes, he ___ the piano for ten years.
items.why: For + a period takes has played with he.

lines: – This one is ___ than that one.
items.why: One-syllable adjectives add -er (and double the g).

lines: – It is ___ than the last one.
items.why: Long adjectives take more + adjective.

lines: – Who is taller, you or Paul?
items.why: Short adjective: tall + -er.

lines: – It is ___ than the one near the station.
items.why: Short adjective: cheap + -er.
Hot doubles the t: hotter.

lines: – This one is ___ expensive than that one.
items.why: Expensive takes more to compare.

lines: – Who is the ___ student in your class?
items.why: The + adjective + -est: tallest.

lines: – What is the best hotel here?
items.why: Long adjectives: the most + adjective.

lines: – It was ___ holiday of my life!
items.why: Good has an irregular superlative: the best.
Superlative needs the + -est: the shortest.

lines: – Which is the ___ month of the year?
items.why: The + adjective + -est: shortest.

lines: – Who is the ___ person you know?
items.why: The + adjective + -est: oldest.

lines: – No, you ___ do your homework first.
items.why: With you: have to + base verb.

lines: – Why is Tim at the office on Sunday?
items.why: With he: has to + base verb.

lines: – You ___ drive fast near the school. It is dangerous.
items.why: Mustn't means it is forbidden.

lines: – Do I have to wear a tie?
– No, you ___. It is a casual party.
items.why: No obligation: don't have to.

lines: – I ___ go now. My bus leaves in five minutes.
items.why: Must + base verb expresses obligation.

lines: – Does she have to work tomorrow?
items.why: Short answer with she: she doesn't.

lines: – When did you move to Lima?
items.why: A finished past time (in 2019) needs the past simple.

lines: – Yes, I ___ it ten minutes ago.
items.why: "Ten minutes ago" is a finished time: past simple.

lines: – Yes, I ___ him since primary school.
items.why: Since + a starting point continues to now: present perfect.

lines: – No, she ___ out an hour ago.
items.why: A time reference with ago needs the past simple.

lines: – Why didn't you answer the phone?
– I ___ a shower when you called.
items.why: An action in progress at a past moment: was + -ing.

lines: – He fell while he ___ down the stairs.
items.why: The longer background action takes the past continuous.

lines: – What ___ you doing at eight last night?
items.why: Past continuous with you: were + -ing.

lines: – Yes, the children ___ in the street.
items.why: Children is plural: were + -ing.

lines: – If it rains, we ___ at home.
items.why: If + present, then will + base verb.

lines: – If you ___ hard, you will pass the exam.
items.why: The if-clause of a real future condition uses the present.

lines: – Shall we go for a walk?
items.why: No will in the if-clause: the weather is nice.

lines: – I won't go if she ___ me.
items.why: The if-clause stays in the present: doesn't invite.

lines: – What would you do if you won the lottery?
– I ___ a house by the sea.
items.why: An imaginary situation: would + base verb.

lines: – If I ___ more time, I would learn another language.
items.why: Unreal present: if + past simple.

lines: – If he ___ taller, he would play basketball.
items.why: In the second conditional we often say were after he.

lines: – If I ___ a good job there, yes.
items.why: The if-clause takes the past simple: got.
Advice: should + base verb.

lines: – Do I need a passport for the trip?
– Yes, you ___ have one. It is required.
items.why: A strong rule: must.

lines: – No, you ___ take it if you don't want to.
items.why: No obligation: don't have to.

lines: – You ___ smoke in the hospital. It is not allowed.
items.why: Prohibition: mustn't.
Passive past: was + past participle.
Passive present singular: is + past participle.
Plural subject: are + past participle.
Passive past: was + made.

lines: – Because she ___ her wallet on the bus.
items.why: The earlier past event takes the past perfect.

lines: – The film ___ when we arrived at the cinema.
items.why: Earlier past action: had + past participle.

lines: – Did you eat lunch with Ben?
– No, he ___ by the time I got there.
items.why: An action done before another past moment: had eaten.

lines: – He ___ a lot since I last saw him.
items.why: Change before a past moment: had changed.

lines: – Do you still play the guitar?
– No, I ___ play it every day, but not now.
items.why: A past habit that stopped: used to + base verb.
After did we use use to.

lines: – My grandfather ___ smoke, but he stopped last year.
items.why: A finished past habit: used to.

lines: – She is used to ___ up early.
items.why: Be used to + -ing means being accustomed.

lines: – She is the girl ___ lives next door.
items.why: For a person as subject we use who.

lines: – Is this the book ___ you told me about?
items.why: For a thing we use that or which.

lines: – It is a person ___ makes bread.
items.why: A person is described with who.

lines: – This is the city ___ I was born.
items.why: For a place we use where.

lines: – Yes, I enjoy ___ for my friends.
items.why: Enjoy is followed by the -ing form.

lines: – I decided ___ a new job last month.
items.why: Decide is followed by the to-infinitive.
Forget + to-infinitive means we did not do the task.
Mind is followed by the -ing form.
A positive statement takes a negative tag with the same verb: isn't it.
A negative statement takes a positive tag: have you.
Present simple positive takes doesn't she.
After Let's the tag is shall we.
In reported speech the present moves back to the past: was.
Reported questions use statement order and a past tense: lived.

lines: – What did the teacher tell you?
– She told me ___ the book home.
items.why: Tell + person + to-infinitive reports an order.

lines: – "I will call you tomorrow," he said.
– He said he ___ me the next day.
items.why: Will becomes would in reported speech.

lines: – I missed the train, so I was late.
– If you ___ earlier, you wouldn't have missed it.
items.why: The if-clause of the third conditional takes the past perfect.

lines: – If it hadn't rained, we ___ to the beach.
items.why: A past unreal result: would have + past participle.

lines: If she would have asked me, I would have helped her.
If she had asked me, I would have helped her.
items.why: Not would have in the if-clause: had asked.

lines: If they hadn't missed the bus, they would have been on time.
If they hadn't missed the bus, they would be on time.
items.why: A wholly past situation needs would have been.

lines: – It is so cold in this flat.
items.why: A wish about the present takes the past form: were.
A regret about the past: if only + past perfect.

lines: I wish I would have more free time.
I wish I had more free time.
items.why: A wish about the present takes the past simple: had.

lines: If only I had listened to her.
If only I would listen to her yesterday.
items.why: A past regret: if only + past perfect.
Future passive: will be + past participle.

lines: – The room ___ right now, so please wait outside.
items.why: Present continuous passive: is being + past participle.
A past event after is said: to have + past participle.

lines: – I don't like ___ what to do.
items.why: After like in the passive we use being + past participle.
Accuse someone of doing something.
Admit is followed by the -ing form.

lines: She suggested me to go to the park.
She suggested going to the park.
items.why: Suggest is not followed by a person + to-infinitive.

lines: He warned me not to touch the wire.
He warned me to not touching the wire.
items.why: Warn + person + (not) to-infinitive.
Provided that means only if.

lines: – We will have the picnic ___ it rains.
items.why: Unless means if not, so it needs a positive verb.
In case means as a precaution.

lines: – ___ you hurry, you will miss the train.
items.why: Unless you hurry means if you don't hurry.
Causative: have + object + past participle.

lines: – I ___ it fixed at the garage.
items.why: Someone else did the work: had it fixed.

lines: – We are going to ___ the house painted next week.
items.why: Causative: have + object + past participle.

lines: – She ___ her photo taken by a professional.
items.why: Causative past: had + object + past participle.

lines: – My brother, ___ lives in Chile, is visiting.
items.why: Non-defining clauses cannot use that; a person takes who.

lines: – The Eiffel Tower, ___ was built in 1889, is in Paris.
items.why: A thing in a non-defining clause takes which.

lines: – Our teacher, ___ car broke down, was late.
items.why: Whose shows possession.

lines: – We stayed in Lisbon, ___ we met some old friends.
items.why: A place in a non-defining clause takes where.
Little is uncountable; a little means some.

lines: – How many friends did you invite?
items.why: A few means some (countable).
Little means almost none for uncountable nouns.
A lot of works with uncountable nouns in positive sentences.

lines: – ___ the rain, we went for a walk.
items.why: Despite is followed by a noun.

lines: – ___ it was cold, he wore a T-shirt.
items.why: Although is followed by a clause.

lines: – I like him. ___, I don't trust him.
items.why: However links two separate sentences.

lines: – She works hard, ___ her sister is lazy.
items.why: Whereas contrasts two clauses.
An action lasting up to a past moment: had been + -ing.

lines: – They ___ for two hours when the bus finally came.
items.why: Duration before a past moment: had been waiting.

lines: – He was out of breath because he ___.
items.why: Cause in the past: had been running.

lines: – How long ___ you been studying when she called?
items.why: Past perfect continuous question: had you been.

lines: – The more you practise, ___ you will be.
items.why: The more ... the + comparative.

lines: – This exam is ___ difficult as the last one.
items.why: Not as ... as shows a lower degree.

lines: – Her English is getting ___ every day.
items.why: Repeated comparative shows gradual change.

lines: – It is twice ___ as expensive as the other one.
items.why: Twice as + adjective + as.
After Never at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

lines: – Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the documents.
items.why: Not only at the start takes inversion with did.

lines: – Hardly ___ the house when it started to rain.
items.why: Hardly requires inversion: had we left.
Rarely at the start takes do/does + subject.

lines: – It was in Cusco ___ we first met.
items.why: An it-cleft for a place uses that.

lines: – ___ annoys me is his constant lateness.
items.why: What starts a wh-cleft.

lines: What I need it is a long holiday.
What I need is a long holiday.
items.why: A what-cleft needs no extra pronoun before is.

lines: It was Maria who solved the problem.
It was Maria who she solved the problem.
items.why: In an it-cleft the relative pronoun replaces the subject.

lines: – ___ I known earlier, I would have acted differently.
items.why: Had + subject replaces if + had.

lines: – ___ you need any help, don't hesitate to ask.
items.why: Should + subject replaces if you should.

lines: – ___ it not for her support, I would have quit.
items.why: Were it not for = if it were not for.

lines: – ___ he to apologise, I might forgive him.
items.why: Were + subject + to replaces if he were to.

lines: – It's high time we ___ the problem seriously.
items.why: It's high time takes the past simple.
I'd rather + subject takes the past simple.

lines: I suggest that he takes a break.
I suggest that he take a break.
items.why: After suggest that, the subjunctive uses the base form.

lines: It is essential that she be present.
It is essential that she is being present.
items.why: After essential that we use the base verb be.

options: Hey, can we move the meeting?
Would it be possible to reschedule the meeting?
items.why: The impersonal conditional with a formal verb is the most formal request.

options: I would like to express my sincere gratitude.
items.why: The formal noun phrase is the most formal way to thank.

options: I'm writing to let you know your order is late.
Just so you know, your order is late.
Hey, your order is a bit late.
I am writing to inform you that your order has been delayed.
items.why: Inform you + has been delayed is the most formal.

options: I regret to inform you that I will be unable to attend.
items.why: Regret to inform you is the most formal way to decline.
